paper_title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: LLM coding agents now edit hardware code and run the compilers, simulators, and synthesis tools that check it. We study them on one such task, building an accelerator for language-model decoder. At each decoding step, decoder reads one token, computes scores over its vocabulary (logits), and updates values that later steps reuse, such as the attention keyvalue cache and the recurrent states of hybrid layers. This persistent state makes errors easy to miss. Suppose hardware cache saves result before the next module has taken it. If that module is busy for few clock cycles, the cache saves the same result again and now holds an entry that should not exist. The token produced at that step is still correct, and the error reaches the output only when later step reads the cache. In small decoder we constructed with this defect, the stored state is first wrong at transaction 2, the logits at transaction 5, and the selected token at transaction 6 (Appendix B.5). test that compares output tokens over the first few steps passes this design. We ask what an agent needs in order to get such state right, and how an evaluator can tell whether it did. Two requirements follow. An agent working within fixed budget needs feedback that points to the faulty update, because an output mismatch several steps later says little about where the error began. The final verdict must also come from tests the agent never saw, because an agent can fit its design to the tests it debugs against. In our runs, 148 agent-built designs pass every public test and fail final acceptance, and when frozen submissions are regraded, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail new sequence or condition within the 32 steps their tests required. AIChipBench (Figure 1) is built around these requirements and has three components. The LLM coding agent is language model run in tool-using harness: it inspects files, writes and revises hardware code, runs lint, simulation, and synthesis, reads test feedback, and submits design within caps on wall time, tool calls, and output tokens. The target, quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, or Llama 3.2 decoder, defines what the hardware must compute. The integer oracle, an executable reference that fixes every arithmetic decision of the target, gives the exact outputs and the exact 2 stored state expected at each transaction, the point at which the hardware accepts transfer and commits its result. Agents write register-transfer-level (RTL) code, which describes what circuit computes and stores on each clock cycle. Synthesis maps that code onto the resources of chip, here field-programmable gate array (FPGA), whose logic and wiring are configured after manufacture. submitted design is frozen and accepted only if it matches the oracle on held-out sequences, resets, and memory stalls, synthesizes, and leaves protected files intact. second track, on power, performance, and area (PPA), starts the agent from correct design and asks it to raise throughput by at least 5% with at most 2% more area while every check still passes. In the chip-design flow, which runs from architecture through RTL, verification, synthesis, and placement and routing to fabrication, the agents work at the RTL stage; their designs are placed and routed afterwards for measurement (Section 5). We evaluate coding agents, which edit, test, and revise over many tool calls, because building decoder is multi-step engineering task. decoder takes thousands of lines of RTL (6,843 to 31,884 in the seven reference designs of the correctness track), and one clean validation-and-synthesis pass on the 0.8B reference takes 162 minutes, so an attempts outcome depends on how the agent edits, tests, and spends its budget as well as on the underlying model. This regime differs from single-shot RTL generation, and its results describe model and its harness together. Earlier benchmarks cover parts of this setting. CVDP grades tool-using agents that work in repository against hidden test harnesses, ChipBench includes hierarchical designs and debugging with simulation waveforms, and Build-A-Chip-Bench follows agents from workload specification to routed layout (Section 5). AIChipBench adds two capabilities aimed at stateful accelerators: an oracle that specifies the committed state of decoder at every transaction, and matched study that varies what public feedback reveals (output mismatches only, flag that state differs, or the first state word that differs) while submissions are frozen and graded independently. Repeated attempts under fixed budgets measure each agents reliability and cost, both when building correct design and, on the PPA track, when optimizing one, with place-and-route and board measurements. Four coding agents make 9,136 attempts, and three results stand out. First, what an agent is told about state largely determines whether it succeeds. Feedback that locates the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agenttask cells of matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 points, and lowers the agent-hours per accepted design from 13.4 to 6.5. It also beats flag that only reports state mismatch in all 12 cells, by 9.4 to 37.5 points, so locating the mismatch helps beyond reporting that state differs (Section 4.2). Second, passing test suite does not establish that design is exact, and output checks in particular miss errors of state. When 144 frozen submissions are regraded, 17 of the 85 sequences that fail within the required 32 steps are wrong only in stored state, so an output check of that length passes them (Section 4.3). Third, correctness is fragile under optimization: more than third of the attempts to speed up correct design end without one (Section 4). An overall score that multiplies the two track scores ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 (Figure 2), and in all 200 random splits of the instances into halves, both halves put the same two agents on top.

sections.title: 2.1 Task shape
sections.content: Each task asks an agent to implement quantized language-model decoder, from embedding lookup to output projection, in synthesizable RTL (Figure 1). The agent works in sandboxed copy of starting workspace, with tools for lint, compilation, simulation, bounded property checks, and synthesis, under caps on wall time, tool calls, and output tokens. An attempt is one fresh agent process in fresh workspace; it ends when the agent submits or reaches cap. What correct design computes is fixed by the tasks numerical contract, the integer reference of Section 1. For each target we fix the integer arithmetic (bit widths, accumulation order, rounding, saturation, and the lookup tables that approximate nonlinear functions), so that one decoding step is an integer state transition (zt, st+1) = Fq(xt, pt, st; ), st = (sGDN , sconv , Kt, Vt, mt), (2.1) from token xt at position pt, persistent state st, and weights to logits zt and the next state. The state holds the recurrent and convolution state of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, attention key and value caches Kt and Vt, and valid lengths and control metadata mt; the GDN parts are empty for attention-only decoders. Each integer in the state is state word. The contract runs as an integer oracle outside the agents workspace; agents can query it but not read its code (Appendix A.1). Public tests in the workspace compare the agents RTL with the oracle, from single operators and layers up to the full decoder and multi-step decoding. By default, failed test reports the first mismatching state word: its layer, token, tensor, and index, and the expected and received integers (full-state feedback). Two weaker settings, used in Section 4.2, report output mismatches only (output-only) or report that state mismatched without locating it (coarse-state). When the agent submits, its RTL is hashed, frozen, and graded on an independent clean copy. submission is accepted only if it passes every gate: = Iintegrity Ipublic Iheldout Isynth Ilocal. The gates are (i) an integrity check on protected files; (ii) the full public suite, rerun with state checks whatever feedback the agent saw; (iii) held-out suite with new quantized weights and token sequences, nonzero cache positions, reset after nonempty token sequence (reset after activity), bounded memory stalls, and parameter reload (Appendix B.1); (iv) synthesis; and (v) for all tasks except the two nano tasks, bounded safety checks on reduced instances of the controller (local checks). Held-out results never return to the agent. On the correctness track, an attempt that ends at cap is not graded and counts as failure. Section 4.3 regrades accepted designs under new conditions. (2.2) An example task. One task asks the agent to adapt supplied accelerator scaffold to the official 24-layer Qwen3.5-0.8B text configuration (Qwen Team, 2026a) (Figure 3). The scaffold is working parameterized accelerator, so the module structure is given, and the agent writes the RTL that fits it to the target. Every task has reference design that passes all gates, so the task can be completed. The nano and Gemma 4 E4B references were written by hand and reviewed independently; for the 0.8B and Llama 3.2 3B references, an agent drafted components that an engineer reviewed, edited, and integrated; the 4B reference was derived from gate-passing submission of model outside the four evaluated agents, with 70 lines changed in its reset sequencing and parameter-loading wrapper (Appendix A.1). sections.title: 2.2 What AIChipBench stresses
sections.content: A decoder task combines five demands. Integer arithmetic to the bit. The contract fixes every rounding and saturation decision. Requantization, for example, rounds to the nearest integer with ties to even and then clips (Appendix B.4), and design with the wrong rounding mode fails the public tests  (Table 14)  . State committed only on accepted transfers. decoding step takes many clock cycles, and modules exchange data through valid/ready handshakes: transfer happens only in cycle in which the senders data is valid and the receiver is ready, and otherwise the sender must hold its data (backpressure). state word may change only when the transfer that produces it is accepted; design that writes state whenever result is valid can commit value twice under backpressure (Appendix B.5). Because designs may pipeline or reorder work, correctness is checked at each transaction, one accepted transfer of an input and its result, and the cycle-level timing is left to the design. State that stays exact across steps and conditions. Later steps read what earlier steps commit, so state defect can surface late, as in the constructed decoder of Section 1 (Appendix B.5). There, scripted repair that guards only the cache payload makes every output exact while the state and commit checks still fail. design must also stay exact when reset after activity, at nonzero cache positions, and when memory responses stall. test that starts from reset at position zero with an always-ready memory exercises none of these. Hardware quality without loss of exactness. In the power, performance, and area (PPA) track (Section 2.4), correct design is the starting point, and the agent must make it faster at nearly fixed area while every correctness check still passes. sections.title: 2.3 Correctness track: tasks and scoring
sections.content: The correctness track  (Table 1)  has twelve tasks on seven targets from three model families: Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026a,c), Gemma 3 and 4 (Google DeepMind, 2025, 2026), and Llama 3.2 (Meta, 2024). Tasks differ in the starting workspace. In construction from interfaces, the workspace supplies module declarations, testbench interfaces, arithmetic components, and supporting files, but no decoder implementation; in scaffold adaptation, it supplies working accelerator to adapt. Tasks also differ in the decoding horizon, the number of decoding steps the tests require. Two tasks use Qwen3.5-nano, our name for compact Qwen-derived configuration with four layers (three GDN, one full attention), width 256, and 4,096-token vocabulary (Appendix C.1): T2 decodes one step and T3 eight recurrent steps. The labels follow an earlier task series in which T1 is single decoder layer (Appendix G). The other ten tasks require 32 steps. Across the twelve tasks, reference designs have 6,843 to 31,884 lines of RTL. scaffold supplies 16,308 to 27,492 of them, and accepted adaptations add median of 1,382 to 2,311 lines; from interfaces, the agent starts with 284 to 746 lines and accepted designs add median of 6,154 to 34,300 (Appendix Table 9). target qualifies when its reference RTL passes every gate and its contract agrees with the FP32 model on at least 99% of pooled top-1 next-token decisions over common prefixes, threshold set by this benchmark. The two conditions are distinct. Exactness is whether RTL reproduces the contract, and it is what agents are graded on. Fidelity is how closely the contract approximates the floating-point model; it is property of the workload, and either can hold without the other (Section 3.3). Qwen3.5-nano falls below the fidelity threshold at 97.22%; we keep it because its tasks measure exactness and its small size keeps repeated attempts affordable. The Gemma 3 4B (text) and Llama 3.2-1B references qualify: each passes all 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases of its 32-step suite, and their contracts agree with FP32 on 99.00% and 99.31% of decisions; both also meet timing (Tables 4 and 70). 6 On this track we report an agents acceptance rate over all attempts, Yi/N , with Wilson 95% interval. We also report agent-hours per accepted design: total agent time, failed attempts included, divided by the number accepted (Appendix A.3). Two diagnostic studies extend the track: feedback study repeats three tasks under weaker feedback (Section 4.2), and controlled matrix varies the horizon, an added state condition, and the budget from one nano scaffold (Section 4.4). sections.title: 2.4 PPA track
sections.content: The PPA track measures hardware quality on four targets: Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B. Every design targets an AMD Alveo U250 FPGA (xcu250-figd2104-2L-e) and is evaluated at 126 MHz target clock, batch size one, an eight-token prompt, and common memory-service model. Throughput is = /C for clock frequency , where counts all elapsed cycles per decoded token, memory stalls included; area is the FPGA look-up-table (LUT) count L; power covers the FPGA and attached DRAM and excludes the host; and energy per token is P/R. An agent starts from the correct reference design and is asked to improve its throughput, resources, or energy efficiency. Attempt counts as improved only if the design stays correct, gains at least 5% throughput, and grows its LUT count by at most 2%: Si = correct I[Ri/R0 1 0.05] I[Li/L0 1 0.02] , (2.3) where R0 and L0 are the evaluators values for the starting design: 3.999 tokens/s and 61.8k LUTs for 0.8B, 0.800 tokens/s and 69.0k LUTs for 4B, 0.940 tokens/s and 74.4k LUTs for Gemma 4 E4B, and 1.120 tokens/s and 66.6k LUTs for Llama 3.2 3B. Energy efficiency is reported but does not enter the criterion. Each agent makes 96 attempts per target. The 0.8B and 4B reference designs are also carried through the backend: we place and route them with three implementation seeds, check timing closure at 126 MHz, and measure power on an FPGA board (Section 3.2). Agent designs are scored on the evaluators throughput, LUT, and energy values; as check, every correct agent design is also placed and routed with three seeds (Section 3.2). The agent edits only the RTL; placement and routing run after it Physical implementation. submits. Designs are implemented with Vivado 2024.1, AMDs placement-and-routing flow for its devices (AMD, 2026b), which maps synthesized design onto the U250s fixed look-up tables, block RAM, DSP slices, and programmable interconnect and produces bitstream. OpenROAD (Ajayi et al., 2019) automates different setting, ASIC physical design: its flow takes RTL for chosen process design kit through floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, and routing to layout of standard cells and memory macros. Vivado is the implementation flow for the U250, on which routed design can be run and its power measured on the board; every routed and board result here is an FPGA result. An ASIC version would need process design kit, cell and memory libraries, and physical verification, and its results would not be comparable with these FPGA numbers (Appendix E.2). sections.title: 3 Results
sections.content: We evaluate four coding agents, Sol 5.6, Astra 6, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, all run through the MathCode harness (Team Math-AI, 2026). Each makes 472 attempts on the correctness track and 384 on the PPA track. The four agents receive the same task instances, starting files, instructions, tools, feedback, and caps; task instance fixes the initial RTL files, quantized parameter arrays, public inputs, and held-out test assignment. The diagnostic studies bring the total to 9,136 attempts (Appendix Table 7). Overall score. Fable 5.1 and Sol 5.6 score 25.0 and 24.5, and Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 score 16.8 and 16.5 (Figure 2); the gap comes mostly from the PPA track. To test whether the order depends on which instances are drawn, we split the matched instances of every task into random halves: both halves rank Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 in all 200 splits, against 17% of splits when the agents outcomes are permuted within instances (p = 0.001; Appendix Table 56). Each track and the controlled matrix also yield an order that recurs across halves, though the orders differ (Appendix D.8). Scoring the PPA factor at the clock each design achieves after place and route gives 23.7 for Sol 5.6, 22.8 for Fable 5.1, 14.9 for Astra 6, and 15.6 for Opus 5.5, and all four differences between an agent of the first pair and one of the second stay below 0.05 after Holm adjustment (Figure 4b, Appendix Table 65).

sections.title: 3.1 Correctness track
sections.content: Sol 5.6 has 61.2% of its attempts accepted, Opus 5.5 55.9%, Astra 6 49.8%, and Fable 5.1 48.3%, at 23.9 to 31.4 agent-hours per accepted design (Appendix Table 53). On matched instances, Sol 5.6 is ahead of Astra 6 and Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 is ahead of Fable 5.1 (Holm-adjusted 0.024; Appendix D.8). About 26% of attempts end at cap without submitting. Between 55 and 70% of attempts pass each suite, but only 48 to 61% pass every gate.

sections.title: 3.3 Reference designs beyond the benchmark targets
sections.content: To test whether the contract and evaluator carry to decoders outside the benchmark, we built reference designs for the attention-only Gemma 2 2B (Google, 2024) and the 64-layer hybrid Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) (Appendix F.1). Table 4 compares them on exactness and fidelity with four references that qualify: Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B, and the correctness-track targets Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B (Section 2.3). Both meet timing  (Table 70)  , and each fails different criterion. Gemma 2 2Bs RTL matches its contract on every case, but the contract agrees with FP32 on only 98.38% of decisions. Seven of eight alternative integer contracts reach the threshold, and higher precision costs hardware: LUTs rise from 58.4k to 84.1k and throughput falls from 1.48 to 0.90 tokens/s (Appendix F.2). Qwen3.6-27Bs contract meets the threshold, but its RTL fails eight public and ten held-out cases even though every operator and layer check passes, so the defects appear only when layers are integrated. Two later revisions reduce the failures to one or two cases; neither passes every check, so Qwen3.6-27B does not qualify.

sections.title: 4.2 Agents do much better when told where state diverges
sections.content: On nano T2, nano T3, and Qwen3.5-0.8B, each agent attempted 32 task instances under each feedback setting; the three attempts on one instance form matched block. Full-state feedback raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agenttask cells, by 25.0 to 46.9 points, and every block-bootstrap interval excludes zero (Appendix Table 34). Pooled, 144, 208, and 295 of 384 attempts are accepted under output-only, coarse-state, and full-state feedback, with nearly equal total agent time, so the cost per accepted design falls from 13.4 [11.3, 16.2] to 6.5 [5.9, 7.3] agent-hours, ratio of 0.49 [0.42, 0.56]. Output-only and full-state feedback differ both in whether state is visible and in whether the mismatch is located. Coarse-state feedback reports state mismatch without locating it, and full-state feedback exceeds it in all 12 cells, by 9.4 to 37.5 points, with intervals that exclude zero in seven. Removing any one of the 96 matched blocks keeps the pooled ratio between 0.48 and 0.50, and in each of the 12 agenttask cells the interval of the full-state ratio lies below one (Figure 5a, Appendix D.4). Accepted designs also arrive earlier: by half the wall cap, 82 of 384 full-state attempts had submitted design that was later accepted, against 67 under coarse-state and 52 under output-only feedback (Appendix D.7). Comparing the two state settings separates finding state defect from repairing it. Among attempts with state defect, agents find it slightly more often under full-state feedback, in 151 of 13 166 after median of 1.35 agent-hours, than when told only that state disagrees, in 142 of 169 after 1.50 hours. Repair differs more: agents repair the defect in 123 of the 166 under full-state feedback, after median of 2.69 hours, and in 87 of the 169 under coarse-state feedback, after 3.22 hours  (Table 37)  . On the constructed decoder of Section 2.2, one Sol 5.6 repair under each setting shows what the agent is told. Full-state feedback reports cache valid count of 4 at transaction 2, where the oracle expects 2; output-only feedback reports logits [12, 12, 6, 5] at transaction 5, where the oracle expects [13, 12, 6, 6]. Both runs make the same one-line change, committing the cache entry only when the output transfer is accepted, and pass the held-out suite (Appendix B.6). The gain splits between reporting that state disagrees and locating where. Full-state feedback adds 151 pooled acceptances over output-only feedback; 64 arise between output-only and coarsestate feedback and 87 between coarse-state and full-state feedback. Both increments are positive in every cell. Full-state exceeds coarse-state feedback by 9.4 to 37.5 points, with intervals that exclude zero in seven of the 12 cells; for the gain of coarse-state over output-only feedback, the intervals exclude zero in only two cells  (Table 35)  .

sections.title: 4.3 Passing a test suite does not establish exactness
sections.content: On the correctness track, 148 designs that pass every public test fail final acceptance, 115 of them on the held-out suite: 25 for Sol, 39 for Opus, 33 for Fable, and 51 for Astra. For the 36 such designs on Gemma 4 E4B, Llama 3.2 3B, and Qwen3.5-4B, the graders primary diagnoses are 13 integration, 13 state/protocol, and 10 arithmetic (Appendix D.1). The gap between what the agent sees pass and what is accepted is wider under output-only feedback: of 384 output-only attempts, 219 submit design that passes every check the agent can see, 199 also pass the full public suite, and 144 are accepted. Accepted designs can also fail under conditions their tests did not cover. We regraded 144 frozen submissions on Qwen3.5-0.8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B, 69 of which had been accepted, together with the three reference designs. Each design decodes eight new token prefixes under each of four conditions (a new prefix alone, nonzero cache positions, reset after activity, and bounded memory stalls) for up to 256 steps, which gives 32 sequences per design. The references stay exact throughout. Of the 69 accepted submissions, 45 fail at least one sequence within the 32 steps their tests required, although 2,123 of their 2,208 sequences stay exact. The failures concentrate in the conditions that exercise state: of the 85 failing sequences, 29 fail under bounded memory stalls, 28 under reset after activity, 19 at nonzero cache positions, and only 9 on new prefix alone. At 256 steps, stalls remain the hardest condition, with 60.6 to 69.9% of sequences exact per target against 75.6 to 86.1% on new prefixes alone  (Table 44)  , and only 20 of the 69 are exact on all eight new prefixes alone, and 482 of the 624 failing sequences first diverge in persistent state, median of four steps before the output does (Figure 5b). Within the required 32 steps, 17 of the 85 failing sequences, and 5 of the 45 failing designs, are wrong in state only, so an output test of that length would pass them. Longer output tests find these defects later: extended to 35 steps, output checks detect 79 sequences and miss 10 that the 32-step state check finds, and at 48 steps they miss none (Figure 5c, Appendix D.6). sections.title: 4.4 Longer horizons lower acceptance, and the budget binds
sections.content: The controlled matrix starts every attempt from one Qwen3.5-nano scaffold and varies the required decoding steps (1 to 16), an added state condition (none, reset after activity, or bounded memory stalls), and multiplier on all three caps. At the 1 budget, pooled acceptance falls from 252 to 115 of 288 attempts between one and 16 required steps, and with no added condition every agent has fewer attempts accepted at 16 steps than at one  (Table 6)  . 1.5 budget lifts the 16-step result to 169 of 288, but acceptance still falls at each longer horizon. On the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks, the same instances at eight and at 32 required steps have 558 and 475 of 1,024 attempts accepted (Appendix D.2). How an added state condition changes the horizon effect depends on the budget. At 0.5, where at most 1 of 96 attempts per cell is accepted at 16 steps, the interaction is positive because acceptance has little room to fall; at 1 it is negative for reset after activity, and the other intervals include zero (Appendix D.5). The budget binds on the correctness track as well: 489 of 1,888 attempts end at cap without submitting (322 on wall time, 105 on tool calls, and 62 on output tokens). Under full-state feedback, caps account for about half of the failures that remain: on the three feedback tasks, 43 of the 89 failed full-state attempts end at cap, and 39 of these 43 had no state defect or had already repaired it. Caps also end 260 of the 465 failed attempts to build full-size decoder from interfaces.

sections.title: 4.5 Optimization often ends without a correct design
sections.content: In the PPA track, 571 of 1,536 attempts end without correct design, 90 to 185 of 384 per agent: 194 submit an incorrect design, and 377 reach cap with RTL that fails the correctness checks. Every one of these attempts started from design that passed every gate. In one such attempt (Figure 6b), Sol 5.6 starts from the correct 0.8B design at 3.999 tokens/s and stops at the tool-call cap with design that fails the correctness checks and runs at 3.803 tokens/s.

(c) An output-only submission passes every check the agent can see and, after the RTL is frozen, fails the full public suite and the held-out suite (Listing 2). resources; physical implementation, which places and routes the design and analyzes its timing and power; and finally deployment on an FPGA or fabrication as an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). Language models have been applied at several of these stages, including RTL generation, verification, EDA scripting, tool orchestration (Liu et al., 2023a; Wu et al., 2024), and the full path from workload specification to routed layout (Gunukula et al., 2026). Given target decoder and fixed module structure, AIChipBenchs agents write, debug, and optimize RTL; the evaluator runs verification and synthesis, and placement and routing follow submission (Section 2.4). Architecture design and high-level synthesis lie upstream. Benchmarks. VerilogEval (Liu et al., 2023b), built from HDLBits (Wong, 2024) problems, RTLLM (Lu et al., 2024) with its 2.0 release (Liu et al., 2024), TuRTLe (Garcia-Gasulla et al., 2025), and RTL-Repo (Allam and Shalan, 2024) ask model to generate or complete module or design and simulate it against references; RTLLM and TuRTLe also score synthesis or PPA. ChipBench (Yu et al., 2026) adds hierarchical and CPU-component generation, debugging, and reference-model generation. CVDP (Pinckney et al., 2025) covers design, verification, debugging, and comprehension, and in its agentic tasks an agent works with tools in repository before hidden harnesses grade the result; LBC-bench (LBC-bench Team, 2025) reports model and agent results on CVDP tasks. Build-A-Chip-Bench (Gunukula et al., 2026), described in blog post, carries agents through architecture and physical design to an ASIC layout scored on PPA. Appendix Table 75 compares what each benchmark grades. AIChipBench shares executable tools and hidden grading with the agentic benchmarks. Within fixed module structure, it measures state-exact correctness of decoder accelerators over decoding steps, the effect of what debugging feedback reveals, and each agents reliability and cost over repeated budgeted attempts. Benchmark sizes count problems, designs, examples, or tasks, units comparable neither across benchmarks nor with agent attempts (Appendix H). The closest feedback study is ChipBenchs, which gives models buggy design with or without simulation waveforms (signals and internal state over time); the waveforms improve results for 8 models and lower them for 13. It differs from ours in information and protocol, so the results are not directly comparable. Architect Labs (Architect Labs, 2026) studies RTL generation with verifiable rewards. Verification across representations. EDASYTH (Yuen and Hoang, 2026) gates transitions among symbolic calculations, simulation, and circuit artifacts, EEBench (atopile, 2026) evaluates electrical engineering designs through simulation and cost, and the large-circuit-model perspective (Chen et al., 2024) studies learning across specifications, RTL, netlists, and layouts. AIChipBench checks one transition, from quantized model to RTL, against an executable state-transition contract.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: AIChipBench tests whether LLM coding agents can build decoder hardware that stays exact, in outputs and committed state, over many decoding steps, and whether they can make correct design faster without breaking it. Its results locate the difficulty in stored state. When accepted designs fail under conditions their tests did not exercise, most of the failing sequences diverge in state before the output does, and output checks of the required length miss defects that state check exposes. Agents, in turn, succeed far more often when they can see that state: feedback that locates the first state mismatch doubles pooled acceptance over output-only feedback, after which caps account for about half of the remaining failures. Correctness is also fragile under optimization, since more than third of attempts to speed up correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and the order holds across random halves of the instances. Debugging tools for hardware agents should therefore report stored state, and final evaluations should test well beyond the development cases. Limitations. Tasks fix the module structure, and agents do not place and route their designs. Graded horizons stop at 32 steps and regrading at 256. Whether feedback on stored state and held-out state conditions helps on other stateful hardware remains to be tested.

All results in this section come from Icarus Verilog simulation of each snapshot on fixed, directed public suite of four cases (24 transactions) and held-out suite of five cases (31 transactions). The seeded defect writes the cache entry and increments the valid count whenever the output is valid, before the output transfer is accepted. Under output backpressure the design therefore commits one token more than once. In the public case with output stalls, the valid count is first wrong at transaction 2, the logits at transaction 5, and the selected token at transaction 6 (Figure 9). It has four layers (three GDN and one attention layer), hidden width 256, intermediate width 768, and vocabulary 4,096. It is the target of the nano correctness-track tasks (T2 and T3), the controlled matrix, and the earlier task series. Reference exactness and fidelity. The nano reference passes all 1,384 public cases. Its contract agrees with FP32 on 1,991 of 2,048 top-1 decisions over common prefixes (97.22%), below the 99% fidelity threshold. During development, the reference moved from 62 of 64 to 64 of 64 exact full-model tests and from 27 of 32 to 32 of 32 exact eight-token sequences, while its operator and single-layer tests stayed exact. The development failures were at integration boundaries, and the arithmetic definition did not change while they were fixed. Reference hardware. The nano target is not part of the PPA track, but its reference design has baseline and an optimized schedule, as the 0.8B and 4B references do (Section 3.2). Table 21 compares the two. The optimized schedule improves throughput by 10.5% and estimated energy efficiency by 7.8%, and energy per token falls from 0.0162 to 0.0150 J. Gains are relative to baseline; efficiency is throughput/power. Paired comparison. Both optimized schedules raise throughput by 12.0% and add about 300 LUTs (under 1%) in the pre-route estimate. After place and route (Appendix E.2), the optimized designs use 61.5k (0.8B) and 69.2k (4B) LUTs, against the estimated 62.1k and 69.3k. Both designs time-multiplex shared compute engine and stream weights from external storage, so the larger model adds computation and memory traffic without proportionally larger datapath. Within each workload, the two schedules use the same arithmetic and therefore have the same fidelity. The optimized schedules raise FPGA-plus-DRAM power by about 3.9%, so the 12.0% throughput gain gives an estimated efficiency gain of 7.8%. Energy per token falls from 2.2456 to 2.0831 (Qwen3.5-0.8B) and from 12.6125 to 11.6964 (Qwen3.5-4B). Evidence levels. We report power at three levels: estimates, post-route reports, and board measurements. Estimates come from power budget, which links power and work counts to energy, or from post-synthesis power report, which assumes clock, voltage, temperature, process, and switching activity. Post-route reports add physical implementation information, and board measurements observe the running design (Appendix E.2). Vendor guidance (AMD, 2026a) emphasizes both switching annotation and implementation information. Sensitivity. Let gR = R1/R0 and gP = P1/P0. The energy-efficiency gain is gR/gP 1, so it vanishes when power rises as much as throughput: the 10.5% throughput gain for Qwen3.5-nano gives no energy benefit if power also rises by 10.5%, and the 12.0% gains for 0.8B and 4B break even at 12.0% power increase. E.2 Physical implementation and board power The baseline and optimized schedules of the 0.8B and 4B reference designs were each placed and routed with three implementation seeds and measured on the board with five repeats per seed (Figure 21, Tables 60 and 61). Every baseline implementation and every optimized 4B implementation meets 126 MHz. The optimized 0.8B design meets it on one of three seeds; the other two close at lower clock, so its mean operating clock is 125.3 MHz and its throughput gain is 11.411.8%. Mean post-route LUT counts change by 0.2% for both workloads, where the estimates of Table 57 showed an increase of about 300 LUTs, and BRAM rises by 2.2% and 1.6%. Measured board power rises by 3.1% (0.8B) and 3.7% (4B), and energy per token falls by 7.8% and 7.1%. The resulting efficiency gains, 8.5% and 7.7%, lie within percentage point of the estimated 7.8%. Paired by seed and repeat, all 15 board pairs of each workload show an efficiency 67 gain, from 3.5% to 13.6% for 0.8B and from 4.7% to 12.4% for 4B, with seed means of 7.59.3% and 6.98.2%. All implementations target the AMD Alveo U250 device xcu250-figd2104-2L-e and were built with Vivado 2024.1, the version recorded in the Vivado logs, timing reports, and bitstream headers. Board power is read from the U250s on-board sensors through XRT 2.16.204 and sums the core (0.85 V), auxiliary (1.8 V), and DRAM (1.2 V) rails, sampled at 1 kHz. Each seed is measured in five non-overlapping 10 windows. The reported board power is the total of the three rails during these windows, the same quantity as the post-route estimates it is compared with; each rails median idle power over the 30 before the workload is recorded and is not subtracted. The memory-service model is cycle-relative: request waits 48 cycles, each 64-byte beat then takes one cycle, bursts have 8 to 16 beats, and the interface delivers at most one beat per cycle at 126 MHz; under the bounded-memory-stall condition of the regrading and the controlled matrix, response delays are drawn uniformly from 0 to 256 cycles. The held-out backpressure test and the local checks use shorter stalls of one to three cycles (Appendix B.1). Further references and agent designs. The nano, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B references were placed and routed with three seeds each and measured on the board with five windows per seed  (Table 58)  . All operate at 126 MHz. Gemma 4 E4B decodes 0.940 tokens/s with 73.6k LUTs and an estimated 10.61 W, Llama 3.2 3B 1.120 tokens/s with 67.1k LUTs and 10.07 W, and nano 365.12 tokens/s with 46.8k LUTs and 5.92 W; the nano rate comes from single prepared transaction. The Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B references were placed and routed with three seeds each and close timing at 126 MHz on every seed: Gemma 3 4B decodes 0.883 tokens/s with 73.5k LUTs and an estimated 10.55 W, and Llama 3.2-1B 2.961 tokens/s with 60.4k LUTs and 8.99 W. Across these eight designs and the three references, mean board power differs from the post-route activity estimate by 0.62 to +3.47%, and seed means by 1.70 to +4.21% (Table 59, Figure 20). Every physical result in this paper comes from the FPGA and ASIC implementation flows. FPGA flow described above. Vivado implementation places synthesized netlist onto the U250s existing resources (look-up tables, flip-flops, block RAM, DSP slices, and programmable interconnect), routes it, checks timing, and writes bitstream (AMD, 2026b). The quantities it yields are resource counts, the clock the routed design achieves, and, on the board, rail power. OpenROAD (Ajayi et al., 2019) and the flows built on it target ASIC design: starting from RTL and process design kit, they synthesize to standard-cell library and carry the design through floorplanning, macro and standard-cell placement, clock-tree synthesis, global and detailed routing, and layout generation in GDSII. Their outputs are cell area, routed timing, congestion, and power for chip that would be fabricated, with design-rule checks before signoff. The two flows therefore answer different questions about the same RTL. The contract, the oracle, and the simulation-based tests are independent of the implementation flow; the PPA criterion of Equation 2.3 is stated in FPGA LUTs at 126 MHz clock. Extending the PPA track to ASICs would require choosing PDK and standard-cell library, generating or selecting memory macros for the caches and weight buffers, writing timing constraints for that process, adding physical verification, and restating the area term in cell area. sections.content: F.1 Configurations and detailed checks for additional decoders The four additional reference designs of Sections 2.3 and 3.3  (Table 4)  are for Gemma 2 2B (Google, 2024) (google/gemma-2-2b), the text decoder of Gemma 3 4B (Google DeepMind, 2025) (google/gemma-3-4b-it), Qwen3.6-27B, and Llama 3.2-1B. Image processing is excluded from the Gemma 3 task. For the three attention-only targets, the GDN and convolution components of st in 76 Equation 2.1 are empty. The Gemma 2 2B public suite, like the suites of the earlier eight-step Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B runs (Appendix D.2), has 1,000 cases on primitive operators, 128 on an attention layer, 128 on complete decoder block, 32 on one-step model execution, 16 on eight-step decoding, and 16 on reset/isolation. Its held-out suite has 16 cases each on new token prefixes, supported nonzero cache positions, reset after activity, bounded in-order stalls, and shape-compatible parameter reload. The 32-step suites of the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks have 1,024 operator cases, 192 on individual layers, 192 on complete decoder block, 64 on one-step execution, 64 on 32-step decoding, and 64 on reset isolation, 1,600 in all, and 48 held-out cases in each of the same five families, 240 in all. On common prefixes, the Gemma 2 2B contract matches FP32 on 1,574 of 1,600 top-1 decisions and the Gemma 3 4B contract on 1,584 (Table 67 gives the percentages by position). Gemma 2 2B therefore misses the 99% fidelity threshold although its RTL matches its integer oracle on every case. Building these reference designs involved no agent attempts. Qwen3.6-27B and Llama 3.2-1B. The Qwen3.6-27B configuration (Qwen Team, 2026b) is dense hybrid decoder with 64 layers, hidden width 5,120, and full-attention layer every fourth layer. Like the Qwen3.5 configurations (Qwen Team, 2026a,c), it has gated attention output, but reusing the Qwen3.5 scaffold still required checking gate arithmetic, state layouts, and address ranges. Its public suite has 1,000 operator cases, 128 GDN-layer cases, 128 full-attention-layer cases, 32 one-step cases, 16 eight-step cases, and 16 reset cases. All operator and layer cases pass, but four one-step and four eight-step cases fail. Table 66 gives its ten held-out failures by condition. Llama 3.2-1B (Meta, 2024) is compact text-only decoder from third family. Its suites have the same allocation as the Gemma 3 4B suites, under its own attention, normalization, and positional contract, and all 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases of its 32-step suite pass. Table 67 gives fidelity by position for the four additional targets, with 200 decisions at each of eight positions. Pooled top-1 agreement is 1,574 of 1,600 for Gemma 2 2B, 1,584 for Gemma 3 4B, 1,584 for Qwen3.6-27B, and 1,589 for Llama 3.2-1B. Only Gemma 2 2B falls below the 99% fidelity threshold. Qwen3.6-27Bs RTL matches its integer oracle on 1,312 of 1,320 public and 70 of 80 held-out cases, Gemma 2 2Bs on all 1,400 cases of its suites, and Gemma 3 4Bs and Llama 3.2-1Bs on all 1,840 of theirs  (Table 4)  .
